items.name: icons
items.title: Icons
items.description: Full re-export of @phosphor-icons/react. Every icon is available under bare and Icon-suffixed names; all weights, sizes, and colors are supported. Arbor's system default weight is bold — Arbor components set it explicitly, and mounting IconProvider at the app root applies it to your own bare icons (Phosphor's built-in default is regular).

useWhen: You need a generic UI glyph (arrow, plus, magnifying glass) inside a button, list row, field, or empty state.
You're placing any Phosphor glyph by name (bare or Icon-suffixed) from @linktr.ee/arbor/icons inside Arbor UI.

You want to set weight, size, or color per icon via Phosphor's standard props. Arbor's system default weight is bold — pass weight='bold' explicitly, or mount IconProvider at the app root so bare icons pick it up (Phosphor's own default is regular).
You need an SVG glyph that inherits currentColor and scales with surrounding type.
notWhen: You need a third-party or Linktree service logo (Spotify, YouTube, TikTok) — use AppIcon.
You need a pressable icon control with hit area and states — wrap it in IconButton.
You want decorative imagery or a photo — reach for Thumbnail or an image element.

disambiguateFrom.distinction: AppIcon renders brand and service logos from the synced SVG set; icons renders generic Phosphor UI glyphs. Pick AppIcon for a recognizable product mark, icons for an interface symbol.
IconButton is an interactive control with states and a hit target; icons is just the glyph you place inside it. Pick IconButton when it must be clickable.
Phosphor ships as individual tree-shakeable React components, not a font file or sprite. Import the named component; there is no glyph-by-class or <use href> step.

items.name: button
items.title: Button
items.description: Action button built on Radix Slot with seven variants, five sizes, two shapes, an optional loading state, and start/end icon slots.

useWhen: The action does something in place — submit a form, confirm a dialog, trigger a state change.
You need a clear visual hierarchy of actions: primary for the main action, secondary/tertiary/ghost for the rest.
You want one component to cover both real buttons and button-styled navigation via the link prop or asChild.
An async action needs in-place feedback — use state="loading" to keep the label width and accessible name.
notWhen: The action is icon-only with no visible label — use IconButton, which requires an aria-label.
It's pure navigation in flowing text — use Link or the link variant, not a filled button.
You need a setting that takes effect immediately on toggle — use Switch, not a Button styled as pressed.
More than one primary button competes in the same view — keep one primary and demote the rest.

disambiguateFrom.distinction: Button shows a text label (optionally with a start/end icon); IconButton is icon-only and forces a required aria-label. Pick IconButton when there is no visible text, Button when a label adds clarity.

Link is a real anchor for navigating between destinations; Button fires an action (click handler, form submit). A button that navigates should keep link semantics — use the link prop (renders an <a>) or Button variant="link" for inline text. Pick Link to go somewhere, Button to do something.
Button fires a one-shot action; a control that holds an on/off setting belongs in Switch, not a Button styled as pressed. Pick Switch for live settings, Button for one-shot actions.

SegmentedControl is a single-select toggle across mutually-exclusive choices that stays visually selected; a row of independent Buttons fires independent actions. Pick SegmentedControl for single-select, Buttons for distinct actions.

items.name: button-group
items.title: Button Group
items.description: Layout container that pairs exactly two related action buttons (e.g. Cancel / Save) with shared sizing and an equal-width, auto-width, or stacked layout. Place the primary action last in a row, or first (top) when stacked; caps at two to reduce cognitive load.

useWhen: You are pairing exactly two related actions, like Cancel / Save or Discard / Update.
The two actions should split a row equally, or stack on a narrow layout.
You want one size applied to both buttons and consistent 8px spacing (12px when stacked).
The actions are independent — each fires its own handler — not a single-select toggle.
notWhen: You need a single-select toggle across mutually-exclusive choices that stays visually selected — use SegmentedControl.
Each option reveals a distinct content panel — use Tabs.
You have one action, or more than two — use a standalone Button and lay it out yourself.
The choice is part of a submitted form — use RadioGroup.

disambiguateFrom.distinction: SegmentedControl is one joined single-select control with aria-pressed segments that change a view immediately; ButtonGroup is a layout that pairs two independent action Buttons with their own radii and handlers. Pick SegmentedControl for single-select, ButtonGroup for a two-action pair.
Tabs navigate between distinct content panels (tablist/tab/tabpanel); ButtonGroup fires actions and owns no panels. Pick Tabs for panel navigation, ButtonGroup for an action pair.

A standalone Button is for a single action or an unrelated set; ButtonGroup adds shared sizing, equal-width or stacked layout, and group semantics for exactly two related actions. Pick ButtonGroup only for a genuine two-action pair.

items.name: link
items.title: Link
items.description: Inline link with three sizes, four semantic color variants, underline controls, and safe external-URL handling. Composes via asChild.

useWhen: Linking to another destination inline in body text or as a standalone text link.
An external link needs safe defaults: target _blank, rel noopener noreferrer, and a trailing external icon.
You want a semantic anchor with accent/primary/secondary/danger color and hover/always/none underline control.
Wrapping a router Link or custom element via asChild while keeping Arbor link styling.
notWhen: The control runs a click handler or submits a form rather than navigating — use Button variant="link".
You need Button's size, shape, or leading-icon API on something that looks like a link — use Button variant="link".
The target is a primary page action or call-to-action — use Button with a filled or accent variant.
Rendering a long-form heading or paragraph that is not navigational — use Text.

disambiguateFrom.distinction: Link is a real anchor for navigation between destinations; Button variant="link" looks like a link but is a button for actions (click handlers, form submit). Pick Link to go somewhere, Button to do something.
Button is a filled/bordered action affordance for primary tasks; Link is lightweight inline text navigation. Use Button for CTAs, Link for in-text or standalone navigation.
Text renders non-interactive typography; Link is an interactive navigational anchor. Use Text for content, Link only when it goes somewhere.
A raw anchor skips Arbor's variants, focus ring, and javascript:/data: href sanitization. Use Link so external and unsafe-URL handling come for free.

items.name: text
items.title: Text
items.description: Typography component spanning Arbor's full type scale. Maps each variant to semantic HTML and composes via asChild for headings, links, and labels.

useWhen: Rendering any text in Arbor's type scale — pick a foundations variant like body-medium-regular or display-large-bold.
You need visual style and semantic element decoupled — set the look with variant, the HTML tag with as.
Wrapping a styled child element via asChild so it inherits the typography without an extra wrapper node.
Applying the right font family automatically — category (hero/display vs title/body/caption) selects the binding.
notWhen: You want a heading by HTML level — variant is visual-only; always set as="h1".."h6" for document structure.
Reaching for deprecated names like title-xl or body-base-emph — use the foundations {category}-{size}-{weight} name.
Styling a Button or Field label — those components own their typography; don't wrap their text in Text.
Needing an illegal tier×weight (caption has no extrabold, title/display have no regular) — it is unrepresentable by design.

disambiguateFrom.distinction: A bare h1/p has no design-system styling; Text applies the foundations type scale. Use Text and set as to control the element.

The React Native Text is still on the legacy abbreviated scale with a different variant union; web Text uses foundations names. Don't assume variant parity across platforms — use the platform's own variant set.

Other systems split into Heading + Text or a Typography component; Arbor unifies all five categories (hero/display/title/body/caption) into one Text with a baked variant. Use Text and pick the category via variant.
Form labels and button text are owned by Field and Button respectively. Use those components; reach for Text only for standalone copy.

items.name: sanitize-href
items.title: sanitizeHref Utility
items.description: Strips dangerous URI protocols (javascript:, data:, vbscript:) from href values. Returns undefined for unsafe inputs.

useWhen: Rendering a user- or CMS-supplied URL into an href to strip javascript:, data:, and vbscript: schemes.
Accepting untrusted link values in a custom anchor or button that Arbor's Link/Button/IconButton don't cover.
You need control-char-aware blocking that catches WHATWG parser bypasses like embedded tabs or null bytes in the scheme.
notWhen: Linking with Arbor Link, Button, or IconButton — they already call sanitizeHref on href/link internally.
You need to escape HTML body content or attributes for XSS — use a full sanitizer like DOMPurify, not this scheme filter.
Validating that a URL is well-formed or reachable — this only blocks dangerous protocols, it does not parse or verify URLs.

disambiguateFrom.distinction: Link is the rendered anchor component and calls sanitizeHref on its href automatically; sanitizeHref is the bare utility. Use Link to render an anchor, sanitizeHref only when building your own.
Both sanitize their link prop internally via sanitizeHref. Use them for clickable navigation; call the utility directly only outside these components.
DOMPurify cleans arbitrary HTML markup; sanitizeHref only filters dangerous URI schemes from a single href string. Pick DOMPurify for rich content, sanitizeHref for link targets.
Those percent-encode URL characters; sanitizeHref instead blocks unsafe protocols and returns undefined. Use encode* for encoding, sanitizeHref for protocol safety.

items.name: cn
items.title: cn Utility
items.description: Class merger extending tailwind-merge with Arbor's color, border, radius, shadow, spacing, height, and typography utilities.

useWhen: Merging or conditionally composing Tailwind class strings inside any Arbor component or app.
Passing a className override to an Arbor component so consumer classes win over defaults.
You need Arbor-aware conflict resolution for color, border, radius, shadow/elevation, spacing, height, or typography utilities.
notWhen: Joining classes with no chance of conflicting Tailwind utilities — plain clsx or a template string is lighter.
Merging vanilla Tailwind in a non-Arbor project — bare tailwind-merge already handles the default scales.
Computing variant styles for a leaf component — define them with class-variance-authority and pass the result through cn.

disambiguateFrom.distinction: clsx only concatenates and dedupes class names; it cannot resolve conflicts. cn runs clsx then tailwind-merge, so a later class beats an earlier one. Use cn when classes might conflict, clsx for plain joining.

Bare tailwind-merge doesn't know Arbor overrides Tailwind's scales (e.g. rounded-lg = 24px) or adds elevation/typography groups, so it mis-merges them. cn is tailwind-merge pre-extended with those groups — always use cn in Arbor.
classnames is the older clsx-equivalent concatenator with the same limitation: no conflict resolution. Reach for cn instead so Arbor utility collisions resolve.
cva builds variant-to-class maps; cn merges arbitrary class strings. They compose — define variants with cva, then pass its output plus className through cn.

items.name: elevation
items.title: Elevation
items.description: Shadow utility for Arbor elevation levels 100–400. Defaults to asChild composition so it adds no wrapper div.

useWhen: Adding an Arbor elevation shadow (levels 100-400) to a surface like a card, toolbar, or floating panel.
Wrapping an existing element with asChild so the shadow applies without injecting an extra div.
Mapping level to intent: 100 list items, 200 emphasized item, 300 fixed toolbar, 400 modal/popover.
Keeping shadows theme-aware (auto opacity bump in dark mode, border replacement in high-contrast).
notWhen: Layering overlays above siblings — that is z-index; use the z-overlay/z-toast utilities, not Elevation.
Shadowing a shape with protrusions like a tooltip arrow — use the drop-elevation-* token classes (filter: drop-shadow).
Reaching for an elevation level you invented — only 100-400 exist; pick the closest semantic level.
Tinting a surface color per depth — Elevation only sets shadow, not background; pair with the right bg-* token yourself.

disambiguateFrom.distinction: Elevation is visual shadow depth; z-index is stacking order in the DOM. Reach for z-overlay/z-toast when one thing must render on top of another, Elevation when something should look raised.

Elevation applies box-shadow, which clips to the element's rectangle; drop-elevation-* uses filter: drop-shadow() to trace child shapes (e.g. tooltip arrows). Use drop-elevation for protruding shapes, Elevation otherwise.
Card is a full surface component with padding, radius, and background; Elevation is a shadow-only utility. Use Card for a content container, Elevation to lift any element.

Some systems convey depth by lightening the surface color (Material 3 tonal elevation). Arbor's Elevation is shadow-based only and does not change background color — use Elevation for the shadow and set the surface color separately.

The legacy 'card' shadow token (16px blur) overlaps elevation-100 (4px blur) but is not the same value. Prefer the Elevation component's levels for new work; keep the legacy token only for existing usages.

items.name: icon-button
items.title: Icon Button
items.description: Icon-only button with six variants, five sizes, and squircle or capsule shape. Requires aria-label for screen readers.

useWhen: A control needs to be icon-only and space is tight (toolbars, headers, card corners, input adornments).
The action is universally recognizable from its glyph alone, like close, search, or more options.
You need a compact same-size button matching Button's variants and sizes but with no text label.
You can supply a descriptive aria-label naming the action.
notWhen: The action benefits from a text label for clarity — use Button with a start/end icon instead.
You are toggling between mutually exclusive views — use SegmentedControl.
You cannot give it a meaningful aria-label — the prop is required and the control is inaccessible without one.
You need a tappable status or category marker, not an action — use Badge.

disambiguateFrom.distinction: Button shows a text label (optionally with an icon); IconButton is icon-only and forces a square footprint plus a required aria-label. Reach for Button whenever a label adds clarity, IconButton when space is tight and the glyph is unambiguous.

SegmentedControl picks one option from a set and stays visually selected; IconButton fires a one-shot action with no persistent selected state. Use SegmentedControl for toggling between views, IconButton for a single action.
Badge is a read-only status/category marker; IconButton is an interactive action control. Use Badge to label state, IconButton when the glyph must be pressable.

A toggle is a two-state on/off control that stays pressed; IconButton has no built-in pressed state. For an on/off icon toggle, manage aria-pressed yourself; for a settings on/off, use Switch instead of IconButton.
A FAB is a screen-anchored primary action common in mobile UIs; Arbor has no FAB. Use an inline IconButton — it has no floating/anchoring behavior.

items.name: icon-list
items.title: Icon List
items.description: Display-only vertical list of icon-led rows: a circular icon medallion, a bold label, and an optional description, with an optional connector for a lightweight timeline. Not interactive — for clickable or step-state rows, use a different component; for columnar data, use a table.

useWhen: You're presenting a short vertical list of icon-led rows for reading — each row a circular icon medallion, a bold label, and optional supporting text (feature lists, amenity lists, what's-included, a trial schedule).
You want a lightweight display timeline: turn on connectors and render as an ordered list (as="ol") for chronological or sequential rows.
The rows are display-only — nothing in a row is clickable, selectable, or reports acted-on progress.
You want the medallion, icon, and type to scale together via one size prop (sm/md/lg) with Arbor tokens.
notWhen: Rows are clickable, selectable, or navigable — that's an interactive list, not this (Icon List stays display-only).
Rows carry step-state you advance or act on (current/complete) — use a Stepper/Timeline, not this.
You're lining up columnar, comparable values (plans, specs) — use a table.
Rows are plain text with no icon medallion — use a generic list.
A row's only content is the medallion with no text label — meaning must live in text, not an icon alone.

disambiguateFrom.distinction: A table presents structured, columnar, comparable data for scanning and analysis; Icon List presents icon-led prose rows for reading. Pick a table when columns and comparison matter; Icon List when each row is an icon medallion + label + optional supporting line.

A generic bulleted/numbered list renders plain text items; Icon List leads each row with a colored icon medallion and adds an optional description. Pick List for plain text, Icon List when the leading icon is part of the content.

A Timeline/Stepper models an ordered process with step-state you act on or advance; Icon List is display-only. Icon List can look like a timeline (connectors + as="ol") but never carries interactive step-state. Pick a Stepper when a step is current/complete/actionable.
A Menu is a trigger-opened list of actions or links with keyboard navigation and roles; Icon List is static content with no interaction. Pick Menu when rows do something.

items.name: tabs
items.title: Tabs
items.description: Tabbed navigation built on Radix UI with five variants (underline, pill, pill-subtle, segmented, segmented-pill) and three sizes.

useWhen: Switching between parallel content panels of equal importance within one page context.
You need real TabsContent panels with tablist/tabpanel a11y — the natural home for URL-anchoring or lazy-mount patterns you wire up yourself.
Showing an enclosed segmented look that still wraps content panels — use the segmented or segmented-pill variant.
notWhen: A panel-less in-place toggle (filter, sort, view density) with no content panel — use SegmentedControl.
Step-by-step or sequential flows — use a progress indicator, not tabs.
Primary page or route navigation — use real routes or site nav, not tabs.
People must compare content across panels at once — keep it on one page instead.

disambiguateFrom.distinction: Tabs reveal distinct TabsContent panels (tablist/tabpanel semantics); SegmentedControl is a panel-less role=group / aria-pressed toggle that re-renders in place. Ask one question: do you have real content panels? Yes → Tabs; no → SegmentedControl. The segmented and segmented-pill variants share the look but keep tab semantics (DL-065).

HeaderBar's embedded tabs are the navigation-only tab slot scoped to the page-chrome header; plain Tabs renders interactive content panels. Use HeaderBar tabs for route navigation in the header, Tabs for content switching in the page body.
The enclosed segmented bar people call a 'content switcher' or 'toggle group' is Tabs variant="segmented" when it wraps panels; reach for SegmentedControl only when there are no panels.
Tabs organize content within a page; they are not a replacement for URL-based site navigation. If destinations are routes, use nav, not Tabs.

items.name: segmented-control
items.title: Segmented Control
items.description: Compact inline control for switching between mutually exclusive options — a view or mode toggle with a sliding selected pill. Reach for Tabs with variant="segmented" instead when the segmented look has to wrap real tab panels; SegmentedControl carries no tab semantics of its own.

useWhen: Switching between presentations of the same content (grid vs list, weekly vs monthly vs yearly).
You have 2-3 tightly related, mutually exclusive options and the change applies immediately.
The control lives outside a form and does not submit a value.
Filtering or sorting the same data set in place, with no confirm step.
notWhen: Selecting an option reveals a distinct content panel or changes the route — use Tabs.
The selection is part of a submitted form or dialog — use RadioGroup.
There are 4 or more options — use Tabs or a Select.
Each option triggers an independent action rather than a selection state — use a row of Buttons.

disambiguateFrom.distinction: Same enclosed pill look as Tabs variant="segmented", but split by semantics not appearance (DL-065): Tabs owns real tabpanel content (and is where you'd wire URL-anchoring or lazy-mount patterns yourself); SegmentedControl is panel-less (role=group + aria-pressed) and only emits a value change. Ask: do you have real content panels? Yes → Tabs; no → SegmentedControl.

RadioGroup is a form field (role=radiogroup, roving tabindex, submitted value) for any number of options; SegmentedControl is a toggle-button group for immediate in-place view switching outside forms. Inside a form → RadioGroup; live view toggle → SegmentedControl.

A row of Buttons fires independent actions and can be pressed non-exclusively; SegmentedControl enforces a single active selection that changes view state. Distinct actions → Buttons; single-select view toggle → SegmentedControl.

Arbor's web SegmentedControl mirrors the iOS sliding-pill lineage, but arbor-native ships tokens only — there is no native component. On React Native, reference the tokens and compose a Pressable-based control.

Material's per-segment background cross-fade and multi-select are deliberately not Arbor's model; Arbor uses a single shared pill that slides and is single-select only. Use SegmentedControl with single-select semantics, not M3 multi-select.

items.name: header-bar
items.title: Header Bar
items.description: Page header bar with title, actions, tabs, and a responsive primary/secondary variant. Supports a declarative context API and emits a headerbar:tab-change event for cross-MFE communication.

useWhen: Building top-of-page chrome for Frontyard pages that needs a consistent title, leading slot, and actions.
Remote MFEs must inject title, actions, or tabs into a host-rendered header without prop-drilling (declarative context API).
You need a desktop/mobile action split or a navigation tab strip that responds to container width, not viewport.
Actions should automatically pick up the toolbar button variant.
notWhen: Building marketing, landing, or other non-standard page layouts — use a plain <header> element instead.
Rendering a header inside a dialog or drawer that already has its own heading — use a plain <header> or set titleAs to h2.
You expect tabs to render content panels below the header — HeaderBar tabs are navigation-only; render content by route or page state.
You only need a static heading with no responsive, federation, or tab behavior — plain <header> is simpler.

disambiguateFrom.distinction: Tabs renders interactive content panels; HeaderBar's embedded tabs are navigation-only (panels are hidden) and emit onTabChange / a headerbar:tab-change event. Use Tabs for in-page panel switching, HeaderBar tabs for route navigation in the header.
There is no standalone Toolbar component — HeaderBar's actions slot auto-applies variant=toolbar to its buttons. Reach for HeaderBar when you want page-level chrome, not a freestanding action row.
A plain <header> is right for marketing/landing layouts or headers inside overlays. HeaderBar is for Frontyard page chrome that needs federation, responsive action splits, or embedded nav tabs.

Overlay surfaces own their heading; nesting HeaderBar inside one risks a duplicate h1. Use the overlay's built-in header or a plain <header> with the appropriate titleAs level, HeaderBar only for page-level chrome.

items.name: field
items.title: Field
items.description: Compound input system with floating labels, addons, actions, counters, and three control variants (filled, outline, elevated). Supports stacked (default) and horizontal (settings-row) layouts.

useWhen: Building a single labeled input (text, textarea, or select) with its message, counter, or addons wired up.
You need floating labels, leading/trailing addons, inline actions, or a character counter on one control.
You want label-to-control association, error/success state, and aria-describedby handled for you.
You want a two-column label/control settings row via Field.Root layout="horizontal".
notWhen: Grouping several related controls under one legend (radio or checkbox lists) — use Fieldset + FieldsetLegend.
Laying out a title/description beside its input on a settings page — use Field.Root layout="horizontal".
Placing a standalone checkbox, switch, or radio group — use those components directly, not Field.Control.
You only need a raw uncontrolled <input> with no label, message, or state styling.
Entering a short fixed-length code (one-time passcode or PIN) — use OneTimePasswordField for segmented entry, auto-advance, and paste distribution, not a Field.Input with maxLength.

disambiguateFrom.distinction: Field wraps one labeled control; Fieldset groups multiple related controls under a shared legend. Reach for Fieldset when the label is a question answered by several inputs, Field for a single control.
SearchInput is a purpose-built search combobox with suggestions and a clear affordance; Field is the general-purpose labeled-input system. Use SearchInput for search, Field for form data entry.

FileInput is a standalone, large drop-area for selecting files to upload; Field is for labeled form inputs. Use FileInput for a prominent dropzone (it replaced the former Field file input), Field for text/select inputs embedded in a form.

What people loosely call a 'text input' or 'form group' maps to Field's compound parts (Field.Root + Field.Label + Field.Control + Field.Input), not a single flat element — compose the parts rather than a bare <input>.

OneTimePasswordField is the segmented one-time-passcode / PIN input (per-box auto-advance, paste distribution, numeric IME); Field is general-purpose free-text entry. Use OneTimePasswordField for fixed-length codes, not a Field.Input with maxLength.

items.name: file-input
items.title: File Input
items.description: File upload dropzone surface for selecting files to upload. A dashed drop target with a cloud-upload glyph, click and keyboard activation, drag-and-drop, plus error and disabled states. Use it as the upload trigger; compose selected-file lists and progress above it.

useWhen: Offering a large, primary drop area for uploading one or more files — drag-and-drop or click to browse.
An empty-state upload surface needs a prompt, an icon, and optional supporting text (accepted types, size limits).
The file picker is the main action on a screen, not one input among several in a form.
You want a slot-based dropzone whose icon, label, and supporting text you can customize.
notWhen: Adding a compact file picker inline alongside other form inputs — use a Field control instead.
Managing already-uploaded files (lists, thumbnails, reordering, progress) — compose those above FileInput; it is the upload trigger only.
You need a general labeled text or select input — use Field.

disambiguateFrom.distinction: FileInput is a standalone, large drop-area for the upload action itself; Field is the compound labeled-input system for form data entry. FileInput replaced the former Field file input — reach for it when the dropzone is prominent, Field when a control sits among other form inputs.

items.name: file-input-item
items.title: File Input Item
items.description: Selected-file row composed above FileInput. Shows the file name with middle truncation that keeps the extension visible, secondary metadata, and idle / loading / error states with a trailing action slot, optional thumbnail preview, and a drag-handle affordance.

useWhen: Listing files a Linker has already selected or uploaded, above a FileInput dropzone.
A row needs to show upload progress, a completed file, or a failed upload with a retry or remove action.
You want the file name to truncate without hiding its extension — the row pins the extension and ellipsizes the stem.
An image upload should preview as a thumbnail tile rather than a generic file glyph.
notWhen: Offering the upload action itself — that is FileInput; this row is what you compose above it.
Rendering a generic list row with an icon and supporting text — use IconList.
You need working drag-and-drop reordering. The drag handle is a visual affordance only; wire your own DnD to [data-drag-handle].

disambiguateFrom.distinction: FileInput is the dropzone — the upload trigger. FileInputItem is one already-selected file, composed above it. FileInput ships no list of its own on purpose (DL-088), so a complete upload UI is FileInput plus one FileInputItem per file.
IconList is display-only icon-led rows for general content. FileInputItem is file-specific: extension-preserving truncation, upload status, thumbnail previews, and a remove action.

items.name: skeleton
items.title: Skeleton
items.description: Loading placeholder with pulse and shimmer animations. Includes Text, Avatar, Button, Input, Card, and ListItem preset compositions.

useWhen: A full page or content area whose layout is known loads, and the wait runs 1-10 seconds.
Several elements load at once — one skeleton beats stacking multiple spinners.
Container-shaped content loads: cards, tiles, structured lists, tables, grids.
You can match the placeholder to real dimensions using a preset (Text, Avatar, Button, Input, Card, ListItem).
notWhen: A single inline action loads, like a save or submit — use Button's loading state (state="loading"), not a skeleton.
Duration is known or exceeds 10 seconds — use a progress bar.
Content arrives in under 1 second — render it directly; a flashing skeleton is more jarring.
Static text (titles like 'Settings') or action components exist before data — render them as-is.

disambiguateFrom.distinction: Skeleton mimics a known layout while a whole region loads; for a single inline action use Button's built-in loading state — Arbor has no standalone Spinner export. Use Skeleton for structured regions, the button loading state for one action.
Skeleton is for indeterminate structural loads; a progress bar communicates measurable advancement toward a known duration. Pick the progress bar past ~10 seconds or when progress is measurable.
Shimmer is not a separate component — it is Skeleton's animation prop (pulse default, shimmer, none). Reach for the Skeleton component, not a standalone shimmer.
Skeleton covers a transient load before data arrives; an empty state is the resolved view when there is genuinely no data. Swap a never-resolving skeleton to an empty or error state.

items.name: use-media-query
items.title: useMediaQuery
items.description: SSR-safe React hook tracking a CSS media query. Exports the BREAKPOINT_MD constant aligned with Tailwind's md: breakpoint.

useWhen: You need JS-side responsive logic that mirrors Tailwind's md: breakpoint — import BREAKPOINT_MD so CSS and JS agree at 768px.
A component must branch behavior (not just styling) on viewport, e.g. render a Drawer on mobile vs a Popover on desktop.
You're in an SSR or hydration context and need a hook that safely returns false on the server until the first effect runs.
You want to react to any CSS media query string (orientation, prefers-reduced-motion, custom widths), not only width breakpoints.
notWhen: Pure visual responsiveness — reach for Tailwind md:/lg: utility classes instead; they avoid the hydration flash this hook has.
You need the exact viewport width in pixels — useMediaQuery only returns a boolean match, write a window.innerWidth listener instead.
Desktop content must be correct on first paint — this hook returns false until after hydration, so desktop briefly sees the mobile branch.

disambiguateFrom.distinction: Tailwind handles styling that changes at a breakpoint with zero JS and no hydration flash; useMediaQuery is for JS logic that must branch (which component to mount, what data to fetch). Prefer Tailwind unless you genuinely need to run code.
BREAKPOINT_MD is the exported '(min-width: 768px)' query string aligned to Tailwind md:, not the hook itself. Pass it into useMediaQuery; use the constant directly only when you need the raw string.

AdaptiveModal is the ready-made overlay switcher built on useMediaQuery (Dialog on desktop, Drawer on mobile). Use AdaptiveModal for that exact overlay pattern, the hook for arbitrary responsive branching.

useMediaQuery wraps matchMedia with SSR safety, React state, a dev-mode invalid-query warning, and event cleanup. Use the hook in React; call matchMedia directly only in non-React or non-reactive one-shot checks.

items.name: alert-dialog
items.title: Alert Dialog
items.description: Binary-confirmation modal (Cancel/Delete, Cancel/OK, Leave/Stay). Enforces two-button footer with no close button. Built on @radix-ui/react-alert-dialog.

useWhen: Confirming a destructive or irreversible action (delete account, remove link) before it runs.
Interrupting flow over unsaved state: "Leave without saving?" with two clear paths.
The decision is binary and the body is text-only — exactly two footer buttons (Cancel + action).
You need to block dismissal until a deliberate choice — no X, escape/outside-click are constrained.
notWhen: The body needs form fields, lists, or rich layout — use the future Modal (Dialog is deprecated).
You need more than two footer buttons or a close (X) affordance — use Modal.
The action is low-stakes and easily undone — confirm inline or surface a Toast with undo instead.
You only need transient, non-blocking feedback — use Toast, not a modal.

disambiguateFrom.distinction: Dialog is the deprecated general modal (role="dialog", optional X, any content, scrollable, outside-click closes). AlertDialog is the canonical binary-confirmation modal (role="alertdialog", no X, text-only, blocks outside-click). Pick AlertDialog for confirmations; don't start new work on Dialog.

Modal is the unscoped future component for form-based and rich-content overlays with flexible footers. AlertDialog is text-only with a fixed two-button footer. Reach for Modal once content goes beyond a yes/no question, AlertDialog for the confirmation itself.

Toast is transient, non-blocking notification (often with undo). AlertDialog blocks the page and demands a choice before continuing. Use Toast for low-stakes feedback, AlertDialog when a deliberate confirmation is required.

Alert is an inline, non-modal status banner that stays in page flow; AlertDialog is a focus-trapping modal overlay. Same word, different surface — pick Alert to inform in place, AlertDialog to interrupt and confirm.

Popover (deprecated) is a non-modal floating panel anchored to a trigger; the page stays interactive. AlertDialog is modal and centered with a scrim. Use AlertDialog for a blocking decision; for contextual extras use RichTooltip or Menu — do not adopt Popover.

items.name: dialog
items.title: Dialog
items.description: Modal dialog built on Radix UI for blocking interactions. Compound API covers trigger, portal, overlay, content, header, footer, title, description, and close.

useWhen: Maintaining or migrating an existing Dialog usage already in the codebase; do not adopt it for new work.
You need the older modal anatomy (any number of footer buttons, optional X close) only until a Modal replacement exists.
notWhen: Confirming a destructive or consequential action (Delete, Leave without saving) — use AlertDialog.
Building any new modal — Dialog is deprecated; use AlertDialog now, or the planned Modal for forms and rich content.
Showing a low-stakes, easily-undone confirmation — use Toast or inline confirmation instead.
Presenting a side panel or non-blocking overlay — use Drawer.

disambiguateFrom.distinction: AlertDialog is the canonical, non-deprecated modal for binary confirmations: role=alertdialog, blocks outside-click, exactly Cancel + Action, no X. Reach for it instead of Dialog for new confirmation work.

Modal is the planned (not-yet-shipped) replacement for Dialog covering form-based and rich-content overlays. When it lands, prefer it over Dialog for complex flows; until then maintain existing Dialog usage only.
Drawer slides in from a screen edge for secondary navigation or panels; Dialog is a centered blocking modal. Pick Drawer when content is a side panel, Dialog for a focused interruption.

Popover (deprecated) is a non-modal anchored overlay that does not trap focus or block the page; Dialog blocks interaction. Both are deprecated — for a blocking task use AlertDialog; for lightweight anchored content use RichTooltip or Menu.
People sometimes call a transient confirmation a snackbar/toast. Toast is a non-blocking notification; Dialog interrupts. Use Toast for low-stakes, undoable feedback rather than a modal.

items.name: adaptive-modal
items.title: AdaptiveModal
items.description: Renders a Drawer below the breakpoint and a Dialog at or above it. Only one branch mounts at a time; state stays external.

useWhen: Content works equally well as a centered dialog and a bottom sheet — confirmations, list pickers, settings toggles, single-field forms.
Mobile is a significant audience and you want a native sheet on phones, a compact dialog on laptops.
You want one shared open state and one parallel content tree across both surfaces.
The two branches stay structurally identical — same title, copy, and buttons, only presentation differs.
notWhen: The interaction is a destructive or consequential confirmation — use AlertDialog on every viewport instead.
The panel is side-anchored (nav, filters, notifications) or scroll-heavy — use Drawer at all sizes.
The surface is primarily desktop — use a single Dialog rather than maintaining two branches.
Mobile and desktop content genuinely diverge — build two separate flows, not one AdaptiveModal.

disambiguateFrom.distinction: Dialog is one centered modal for all viewports; AdaptiveModal swaps to a Drawer below the breakpoint. Reach for Dialog when desktop is the only target, AdaptiveModal when mobile deserves a sheet.

Drawer is an anchored sheet at every size; AdaptiveModal is the desktop Dialog branch wrapped around a Drawer. Use Drawer alone for anchored or scroll-heavy panels, AdaptiveModal for centered-on-desktop content.
AlertDialog enforces role=alertdialog, blocks outside-click, and a binary footer on all viewports; never wrap it in AdaptiveModal. Use AlertDialog directly for destructive confirmations.

useMediaQuery is the raw breakpoint primitive AdaptiveModal is built on. Use the hook when you need a boolean for arbitrary responsive logic, AdaptiveModal when you specifically want a dialog/sheet switcher.
Other systems call this pattern ResponsiveDialog or a single dialog with CSS visibility swaps. Arbor's AdaptiveModal mounts only one branch and shares external state — pick it for the same intent.

items.name: radio
items.title: Radio
items.description: Single-select controls built on Radix UI — the canonical Radio (control) and RadioItem (control + label + description), plus RadioButton selectable surfaces (compact, pill, squircle, card).

useWhen: Picking exactly one option from 2-6 mutually exclusive choices that all benefit from being visible at once.
Nearly every radio group — RadioItem (control + label + optional description) is the default.
Choices carry supporting descriptions that help someone decide between them.
You're composing your own label and layout, so you want the bare Radio control.
notWhen: More than one option can be selected at once — use Checkbox instead.
7+ options, or space is tight, or choices are familiar and low-stakes — use Select.
Switching a view or mode inline (Day/Week/Month) where the choice is a reversible toggle — use SegmentedControl.
Reaching for the legacy RadioButton pill/card/squircle surfaces in new work — they are retained only for existing Frontyard consumers.

disambiguateFrom.distinction: Both pick one value; Radio shows every answer at once, Select hides them behind one trigger. Use Radio for 2-6 visible options, Select for 7+ or tight space.

Radio asks a form question with a label/description slot; SegmentedControl is a compact inline view toggle with no form semantics. Pick Radio for a form choice, SegmentedControl for switching a view/mode.
Radio is single-select within a group; Checkbox is independent on/off per item. Pick Radio when exactly one option applies, Checkbox when several can.
RadioButton's pill/card/squircle selectable surfaces predate the canonical Radio and are kept only for existing consumers; new work should use Radio/RadioItem.

People confuse a two-option radio with a switch; a Switch is a binary on/off for one setting, a Radio group is a choice between distinct named options. Pick Switch for enable/disable, Radio for either/or.

items.name: radio-group
items.title: Radio Group (deprecated alias)
items.description: Deprecated alias of `radio` — kept so `npx shadcn add radio-group` keeps resolving during the rename window. Removed in 16.0.0; install `radio` instead.

useWhen: You are migrating an existing `npx shadcn add radio-group` install and need it to keep resolving during the rename window.
You hit a legacy reference to `radio-group` and need to know it now maps to the `radio` component.
notWhen: You are starting new work — install `radio` instead; it ships the same RadioGroup, Radio, and RadioItem.
You want the canonical single-select control with label and description — reach for RadioItem inside a RadioGroup.
You want a component named `radio-group` to be the source of truth — it is only an alias pointing at `radio`.

disambiguateFrom.distinction: `radio` is the real, supported registry entry (RadioGroup + Radio + RadioItem); `radio-group` is just a deprecated alias pointing at the same source. Install `radio`, not `radio-group`.
The `RadioGroup` React export is the live Radix container you compose with; `radio-group` is a registry install-name alias, not a distinct component. Import RadioGroup from the `radio` install.

RadioItem is the default single-option control (control + label + description) you place inside a group; `radio-group` is only the deprecated install alias for the whole family. Use RadioItem for options, install via `radio`.

items.name: checkbox
items.title: Checkbox
items.description: Checkbox built on Radix UI with checked, unchecked, and indeterminate states. Theme-aware inverse fill and a press-scale animation.

useWhen: Letting people pick any number of options in a list, or none — multi-select and opt-in choices.
Capturing explicit consent before a form submits, like agreeing to terms.
A parent control needs an indeterminate state to reflect partially-selected children.
Selecting table rows or filter items where the effect is deferred until submit or apply.
notWhen: The setting takes effect immediately on toggle — use Switch instead.
Choosing exactly one of several mutually exclusive options — use RadioGroup.
You need an error or validation state on an on/off toggle — Switch has none; use Checkbox or rephrase.
Grouping several checkboxes with a shared label — wrap them in Fieldset + FieldsetLegend.

disambiguateFrom.distinction: Switch is for an on/off setting that applies immediately; Checkbox is for selection or opt-in whose effect is usually deferred to submit. Switch has no indeterminate or error state — pick Checkbox when you need either, Switch for live settings.
RadioGroup picks exactly one of N mutually exclusive options; a checkbox group lets each option be toggled independently. Use RadioGroup when only one answer is valid, Checkbox when several can be.

A 'toggle' often means a pressed/unpressed button that holds visual state; Checkbox is a form input that submits a value. Arbor has no Toggle component — use Checkbox for form data, SegmentedControl or aria-pressed for in-context pressed actions.

items.name: collapsible
items.title: Collapsible
items.description: Animated show/hide region built on Radix UI. Supports controlled and uncontrolled modes; honors prefers-reduced-motion.

useWhen: Revealing a single supplementary section the page reads fine without (advanced settings, read more, show filters).
You need an animated height transition on open/close that respects prefers-reduced-motion.
You want a controlled or uncontrolled disclosure with a trigger plus one content panel.
Composing an accordion: lift open state to the parent across several Collapsibles for one-open-at-a-time.
notWhen: The content is essential to understanding the page — show it inline instead of hiding it.
You need many grouped sections expanded at once — compose multiple Collapsibles rather than one.
A static show/hide with no animation suffices — native details/summary is simpler.
Hiding navigation between distinct views — use Tabs; deep hierarchies hurt keyboard nav.

disambiguateFrom.distinction: Arbor ships no Accordion component; build accordion behavior by grouping Collapsibles and lifting open state to the parent. Reach for Collapsible, not a missing Accordion.

Native details/summary is the same disclosure pattern but has no animated height transition or controlled state. Pick Collapsible when you need animation or controlled open, native when a plain static toggle is enough.
Tabs switch between mutually exclusive panels in a fixed slot; Collapsible expands optional content below a trigger. Use Tabs for view switching, Collapsible for reveal-in-place.

Popover (deprecated) floats content in a portal anchored to a trigger; Collapsible expands content inline in document flow, pushing siblings down. Use Collapsible for persistent inline reveal; for transient overlays use RichTooltip or Menu — do not adopt Popover.

items.name: popover
items.title: Popover
items.description: Deprecated — shipped without an approved design (DS-290); do not use for new UI. Floating content surface built on Radix UI with default and inverse variants, configurable side and align, and portal rendering.

useWhen: Maintaining or migrating an existing Popover usage already in the codebase; do not adopt it for new work.
You need a click-anchored non-modal panel only until the Design System team lands an approved design for one.
notWhen: Building any new anchored panel — Popover shipped without an approved design (DS-290) and is deprecated. Route to RichTooltip (rich hover or click-nudge content), Tooltip (plain text hints), Menu (action lists), or AlertDialog (blocking confirmations); escalate anything else to the Design System team.
The content is a brief, non-interactive label shown on hover or focus — use Tooltip or RichTooltip.
It opens on hover rather than click — use RichTooltip.
It is only a list of action items needing arrow-key navigation — use Menu.
The task must be completed or acknowledged before continuing, or needs a focus trap — use AlertDialog.

disambiguateFrom.distinction: RichTooltip opens on hover/focus with a curated title/description layout; Popover (deprecated) opens on click and holds free-form interactive content. Reach for RichTooltip for hover content; do not adopt Popover for new click-anchored panels — escalate to the Design System team.

Tooltip is a plain-text label (role=tooltip) shown on hover/focus and never holds interactive content; Popover (deprecated) is a click-activated role=dialog surface. Just a label? Tooltip. Interactive content? Use Menu for action lists or escalate to the Design System team.

Menu is a role=menu action list with arrow-key navigation; Popover (deprecated) held free-form Tab-navigable content. Action items go in Menu; for free-form anchored panels there is no approved component — escalate to the Design System team.

AlertDialog is modal, centered, and focus-trapped for tasks requiring completion or confirmation; Popover (deprecated) is non-modal and anchored to its trigger. Needing modal behavior means you want AlertDialog.

HoverCard is a read-only hover-activated preview card (a Radix primitive not in Arbor); for a hover preview use RichTooltip. Popover (deprecated) was the click-activated equivalent — do not adopt it for new work.

items.name: rich-tooltip
items.title: RichTooltip
items.description: Click-triggered, content-rich tooltip built on Radix Popover (not Tooltip). Use for onboarding nudges and contextual education; theme-aware inverse styling.

useWhen: Showing a click-triggered nudge with a title plus description that persists until dismissed.
Delivering contextual education or onboarding hints anchored to a specific control.
You need a dismiss (close) button and theme-aware inverse styling on a small overlay.
Content stays short — a heading and one or two lines — and is supplementary, not required.
notWhen: The content is one short text phrase shown on hover or focus — use Tooltip.

The overlay holds arbitrary interactive content like links, forms, or menus — use Menu for action lists; for a free-form anchored panel there is no approved component (Popover is deprecated) — escalate to the Design System team.
The message blocks the page and demands a decision — use Dialog or AlertDialog.
The information is required to complete the task — put it in always-visible helper text instead.

disambiguateFrom.distinction: Tooltip is an ephemeral, hover/focus-triggered plain-text label with no interactive content; RichTooltip is click-triggered, persistent, and carries a title, description, icon, and dismiss button. Pick Tooltip for a one-line hint, RichTooltip for a structured nudge.

Both are built on Radix Popover and persist on click, but RichTooltip is a curated title/description/close layout with inverse styling; Popover (deprecated) is a generic slot for any content tree. Pick RichTooltip for a fixed nudge layout; do not adopt Popover for free-form content — escalate to the Design System team.

Dialog is a focus-trapping modal for content that blocks the page and requires a decision; RichTooltip is a lightweight, non-blocking overlay anchored to a trigger. Pick Dialog when the page should be inert behind it, RichTooltip for in-place education.

A toast (sometimes called a snackbar) is a transient, system-initiated message not anchored to any control; RichTooltip is user-initiated and anchored to a specific trigger. Pick Toast for ephemeral status feedback, RichTooltip for in-place education.

items.name: tooltip
items.title: Tooltip
items.description: Hover-triggered label built on Radix UI with inverse styling, configurable positioning, and prefers-reduced-motion support.

useWhen: Labeling an icon-only button or control whose action has no visible text.
Adding a keyboard shortcut hint to an action that already has a visible label.
Giving a short supplementary field hint that helps but is not required to finish the task.
Explaining a truncated label, short code, or symbol on hover or keyboard focus.
notWhen: Information is required to complete a task — use always-visible helper text or a Field description.
Content has links, buttons, or form fields — use Menu for action lists or escalate to the Design System team (Popover is deprecated).
Content needs a title, description, and dismiss button that persists — use RichTooltip.
Triggering on a disabled button or non-focusable div — keyboard people never see it.

disambiguateFrom.distinction: RichTooltip is click-triggered, persists until dismissed, and holds a title + description + close button; Tooltip is hover/focus, ephemeral, plain text only. Pick Tooltip for a one-line label, RichTooltip for an onboarding nudge.

Popover (deprecated) holds arbitrary interactive content and moves focus into itself; Tooltip content is never focusable. Tooltip is for a static label; the moment content has something to click, use Menu or escalate to the Design System team.

HoverCard previews rich content (avatar, bio, stats) on hover, but Arbor has no HoverCard yet; Tooltip is a short text label. For a hover-triggered preview today use RichTooltip, Tooltip for naming an action.
The browser title tooltip has uncontrollable timing, no styling, and inconsistent screen-reader support. Use Arbor Tooltip for styled, accessible hints — and drop title to avoid a double tooltip.

items.name: select
items.title: Select
items.description: Dropdown select built on Radix UI with outline and filled triggers across three sizes. Integrates with Field for form usage.

useWhen: Picking one option from a list of 4 or more, where you want Arbor styling on the menu.
Options need grouping with labels, custom rendering (icons, descriptions), or popper positioning.
The trigger should match Arbor's outline or filled input styling across sm, md, or lg sizes.
Wrapping in Field for a labeled, validated form control via FieldSelect.
notWhen: The form is simple or mobile-first and OS-native pickers serve better — use NativeSelect.
There are fewer than 4 options — use RadioGroup or SegmentedControl.
People need to search, filter, or create entries in a long list — use Combobox.
Multiple values can be selected at once — Select is single-value only.

disambiguateFrom.distinction: NativeSelect wraps the browser <select> for platform-native pickers and dense forms; Select is the Radix-based custom listbox for grouped options and Arbor-styled menus. Pick NativeSelect for simple mobile forms, Select for rich grouped UX.
SegmentedControl shows all 2-5 options at once as a single-choice toggle; Select hides options behind a trigger. Use SegmentedControl for few always-visible choices, Select for longer lists.
A Combobox lets you type to filter a long list and keeps the selection as a value; Select only picks from a short fixed list with no typing. Roughly 10+ options or any filtering need → Combobox.

items.name: badge
items.title: Badge
items.description: Inline label for status, metadata, and classification. Composes Status, Plan, and Notification specialized badges across nine variants and three emphasis levels.

useWhen: Labeling status, metadata, or classification inline next to a row title or icon (1-2 words).
Showing one primary signal per item across eight semantic variants (success, danger, warning, info, etc.).
Rendering a status pill via StatusBadge or a plan/tier label via PlanBadge.
Showing an online/offline state with a dot-only badge plus an aria-label.
notWhen: Showing a numeric unread or new count — use NotificationBadge (circular, role=status, auto-hides at 0).
Needing dismiss, toggle-select, or removable filter behavior — that's Chip.
Making the whole thing clickable as a filter or link — use Button variant=ghost or a real link.
Surfacing page-level status with a headline and description — use Alert.

disambiguateFrom.distinction: NotificationBadge is a circular numeric count (role=status, auto-hides at 0); Badge is a text/dot status pill. Pick NotificationBadge for unread counts, Badge for state labels.
A chip is interactive — dismissible or toggle-selectable. Badge is strictly read-only with zero focusable descendants. If people can de-select or remove it, use Chip; if it only informs, use Badge.
Alert is a page-level status block with icon, headline, description, and optional dismiss; Badge is a compact inline indicator. Use Alert for 'Payment failed', Badge for 'Active'.
Avatar represents a person or account image; Badge labels words, counts, or status. Pick Avatar for identity, Badge for a status/category label — and AvatarBadge for a presence dot on an Avatar.
Plain inline text carries three or more metadata dimensions on one row; Badge carries only the single primary signal. Don't stack multiple badges — use inline text for the rest.

items.name: indicator-badge
items.title: Indicator Badge
items.description: Communicates presence, activity state, or a count. Renders as a dot for binary states (active/online/error) or a count bubble for notification quantities, with a custom-color escape hatch for off-system use.

useWhen: Showing a numeric notification count (unread, new) as a small bubble that auto-hides at 0 and caps as '{max}+'.
Showing a binary presence or activity state (active, online, error) as a 6px dot.
Needing an off-system custom color for a state outside the built-in notification color.
notWhen: Labeling status, plan, or metadata with text — that's Badge (StatusBadge / PlanBadge).
Surfacing page-level status with a headline and description — use Alert.
Putting descriptive words inside the indicator — IndicatorBadge holds a count or nothing, never a text label.

disambiguateFrom.distinction: Badge is a label — a text/dot status, plan, or metadata pill. IndicatorBadge is an indicator — a dot for a binary state or a count bubble for a quantity, with no text label inside. Pick Badge for 'Active', IndicatorBadge for a red '3'.

NotificationBadge is the older count bubble on Badge (subtle fill); IndicatorBadge supersedes it with the saturated notification color that matches Figma, plus dot and custom-color modes. Use IndicatorBadge for new work.
AvatarBadge is the presence dot positioned on an Avatar; IndicatorBadge is the standalone indicator. Use AvatarBadge when it overlays an avatar, IndicatorBadge elsewhere.

items.name: chip
items.title: Chip
items.description: Interactive compact control for filters and dismissible tags. Toggle mode renders an aria-pressed filter pill; dismissible mode adds a trailing remove button. For read-only metadata, use Badge.

useWhen: Toggling a filter on and off as a compact pill — the whole chip is an aria-pressed button (pass onSelectedChange).
Showing applied tags or filters people can remove — the trailing remove button is the only tab stop (pass onRemove + removeLabel).
Rendering selected values inside an input, like Combobox multi-select chips — static mode, with interaction semantics supplied by the composing component.
Compact filter rows where several independent chips can be selected at once.
notWhen: Labeling read-only status, plan, or metadata — that's Badge (zero focusable descendants).
Choosing exactly one option from a mutually exclusive set — use SegmentedControl (2-5 options) or RadioGroup.
Building a filter button that opens a menu and shows an active-filter count — compose Button + Menu + IndicatorBadge; Chip deliberately doesn't absorb that trigger pattern.
Showing a numeric notification count — use IndicatorBadge.

disambiguateFrom.distinction: Badge is strictly read-only metadata; Chip is interactive — toggleable or dismissible. If people can select, de-select, or remove it, it's a Chip; if it only informs, it's a Badge.

SegmentedControl is a single-choice control where exactly one segment is always active; Chips are independent toggles where zero, one, or many can be selected. Pick SegmentedControl for view switching, Chips for additive filtering.

A filter button (Figma's multi-filter chip: dark fill + count + caret) is a dropdown trigger, not a toggle — compose Button + Menu + IndicatorBadge. Chip toggles or dismisses in place and never opens a menu.
IndicatorBadge is a tiny read-only count/dot indicator; Chip is an interactive pill with a text label. A count inside a filter button comes from IndicatorBadge, not from a Chip.

items.name: combobox
items.title: Combobox
items.description: Searchable selection built on Base UI — a text input that filters an option list and keeps a persistent value. Single mode fills the input; multiple mode renders selections as dismissible Chips. Composes with Field for label, error state, and layout.

useWhen: Selecting from a long list (roughly 10+ options) where typing to filter beats scanning — assignees, tags, countries, links.
Multi-select tagging where selections should render as dismissible chips inside the input (pass multiple).
Async or remote option lists — pass filter={null} and drive the list from your own query results.
A selection needs a persistent value bound to a form (name renders a hidden input) with full Field label, error, and layout integration.
notWhen: Picking from a short static list (under ~10 options) with no filtering need — use Select or NativeSelect.
Navigational search where people visit a result rather than keep a selected value — use SearchInput.
Searching for actions or commands (a command palette) — out of Combobox's scope by design.
Choosing among 2-5 always-visible options — use RadioGroup or SegmentedControl.

disambiguateFrom.distinction: Select is a trigger button over a fixed list — no typing, value shown on the trigger. Combobox is a text input that filters options and keeps a persistent value. If people would want to type, it's a Combobox.

SearchInput is navigational — type, pick a result, go there; nothing stays selected (a <search> landmark). Combobox is selectional — the chosen value persists in the input (single) or as chips (multiple) and submits with forms.
NativeSelect is the OS-native picker for simple forms; it has no filtering beyond browser typeahead. Reach for Combobox when the list is long enough that type-to-filter matters.
Menu hosts actions; Combobox hosts a selection. Combobox deliberately never absorbs command-palette behavior — options are values, not commands.

items.name: search-bar
items.title: Search Bar
items.description: A search-specific text input for filtering, querying, or navigating content in place — a named ergonomic recipe over Field with a leading magnifying-glass, an optional clear (×) button, and Escape-to-clear. No suggestion dropdown (use Combobox for a persistent value, or SearchBar + an anchored Menu to navigate) and no error state (surface "No results" in the results region).

useWhen: Letting someone type a query to filter, search, or narrow content that renders in place (a list, table, grid, or results region).
A search-entry control needs a leading magnifying-glass and an optional clear (×) without hand-wiring them, plus Escape-to-clear.
The field is a self-contained search control — a toolbar/header search, a list filter, a page search — not one input among several in a data-entry form.
notWhen: Typing should reveal a dropdown of suggestions to pick from — use Combobox (selectable value persists) or SearchBar + an anchored Menu (navigational). Do not rebuild the deprecated SearchInput.
The value is form data entered and submitted (name, URL, email) — use Field plus Field.Input.
Choosing from a fixed, static option set — use Select or NativeSelect.
You need an error/validation state — search has none; surface "No results" in the results region instead.

disambiguateFrom.distinction: Field is the compound labeled-input for form data entry; SearchBar is a search-specific recipe over Field with a built-in leading glass, clear button, Escape-to-clear, and no error state. Entering data to submit? Field. Querying/filtering content in place? SearchBar.

Combobox is a type-to-filter input with a listbox popup whose selected value persists and submits with forms; SearchBar is the text entry only — no dropdown, nothing selected. Need a kept, selectable value? Combobox. Just the query field? SearchBar.
SearchInput is the deprecated search-with-suggestions dropdown compound. For plain text search use SearchBar; for suggestions use Combobox (selectable) or SearchBar + an anchored Menu (navigational).
Select picks from a fixed, static option set; SearchBar searches free text over dynamic content. Fixed options? Select. Free-text query? SearchBar.

items.name: divider
items.title: Divider
items.description: Visual separator built on Radix Separator with horizontal or vertical orientation and an optional inline label (e.g. "or").

useWhen: Separating content groups or stacked rows with a thin horizontal or vertical line.
Splitting two sections of inline content with a centered label like 'or' between auth options.
Marking a meaningful boundary for screen readers — pass decorative={false} for role="separator".
notWhen: Separating items inside a Select — use SelectDivider instead.
Adding empty space between elements — use gap or spacing tokens, not a Divider.
Drawing a box outline or grouping into a panel — use a bordered container instead.
Underlining or boxing a heading for emphasis — use typography tokens.

disambiguateFrom.distinction: SelectDivider is a listbox-scoped separator with the right insets and roles; Divider is the standalone separator for page and layout content. Pick SelectDivider inside a select, Divider everywhere else.

Separator is the deprecated alias for Divider (renamed in v13.0.0; still exported as a deprecated alias today, pending removal). Always use Divider in new code, and run the separator-to-divider codemod to migrate.
Divider is the Arbor-tokenized, orientation- and label-aware version of a horizontal rule; reach for Divider, not a raw <hr>, so it picks up theme tokens and ARIA.
A border wraps or outlines an element; a Divider is a freestanding line between two elements. Use a container border to enclose content, a Divider to split it.

items.name: backdrop
items.title: Backdrop
items.description: Translucent scrim that dims UI behind a modal, sheet, or drawer. Composes with Radix overlay primitives via asChild.

useWhen: Building a custom modal, sheet, or drawer that needs a translucent scrim dimming the UI behind it.
Slotting a shared scrim into a Radix overlay primitive via asChild so Dialog/Drawer share one backdrop look.
Dimming a dark surface — pass inverted to render the light scrim instead of the default dark one.
notWhen: Showing a standard modal — use Dialog or AlertDialog; they already render Backdrop inside their Radix Overlay.
Showing a side panel — use Drawer, which composes the scrim for you.
Needing focus trap, escape-to-close, or click-outside dismissal — Backdrop is presentation only (aria-hidden div); wire those via the Radix overlay it composes into.
Frosting a Popover or Button surface — use the glass material axis (.glass-frosted), not the dimming scrim.

disambiguateFrom.distinction: Dialog is a full Radix-driven modal with focus trap and DialogOverlay (which itself renders Backdrop asChild); Backdrop is just the dimming scrim. Reach for Dialog for a complete modal, Backdrop only when composing your own overlay.
Drawer is a sliding panel that already includes the scrim via DrawerOverlay; Backdrop is the bare scrim it builds on. Pick Drawer for a panel, Backdrop only for custom overlays.
What Material Design and other systems call a scrim is exactly this component in Arbor — it is named Backdrop. Same concept, use Backdrop.
The glass material axis frosts a content surface (Popover, Button) so what is behind shows through; Backdrop dims the whole viewport behind a modal. Use material for frosted UI, Backdrop for dimming.

items.name: switch
items.title: Switch
items.description: Toggle switch built on Radix UI with compact and neutral options, an optional inline label, and animated track-and-thumb.

useWhen: A single binary setting takes effect immediately, like enabling notifications or dark mode.
The on/off state maps to a real-time toggle rather than a value submitted with a form.
You need a compact toggle (set compact) or a neutral ink track instead of the success-green active state.
An inline label sits beside the control via the label prop, wired with htmlFor.
notWhen: The choice is opt-in or deferred until form submit, or needs an indeterminate state — use Checkbox.
You need validation or an error state — Switch has none by design; use Checkbox.
People pick one of several mutually exclusive options — use RadioGroup.
An icon-only control triggers an action rather than holding state — use IconButton.

disambiguateFrom.distinction: Switch is on/off with immediate effect and no error state; Checkbox is selection/opt-in, supports indeterminate and validation. Pick Switch for live settings, Checkbox for deferred form submission.
Switch toggles one binary state; RadioGroup picks one of N mutually exclusive options. Use RadioGroup when there are more than two choices, Switch for a single on/off.
Button fires a one-shot action; Switch holds an on/off setting that applies immediately. Pick Switch for live settings, Button for actions — don't style a Button as a pressed toggle.

A 'toggle' often means a pressed/unpressed button (IconButton or SegmentedControl in Arbor); Switch is the labeled on/off setting control. Pick Switch for settings, a pressed-state control for toolbar actions.

items.name: toggle
items.title: Toggle
items.description: An icon-only, binary pressable control (button with aria-pressed) rendered as a switch-shaped sliding pill. Two icons show the off/on states of one concept and the thumb slides over the active one. For toolbar modes and binary view switches — not form settings (use Switch) or picking one of several labeled views (use SegmentedControl).

useWhen: A single binary mode is switched on/off on the current surface, like mute/unmute or live-preview on/off.
The control is icon-only and the two icons represent the off and on states of one concept.
You need a compact toolbar-style control whose state is held (pressed), not a one-shot action.
The change applies immediately in place and is not a value submitted with a form.
notWhen: The setting is a saved on/off preference in a form — use Switch (role=switch), Toggle is for modes not settings.
People pick one of several labeled, mutually exclusive views (grid/list, day/week) — use SegmentedControl.
The control fires a one-shot action with no held state — use Button or IconButton.
You need a visible text label beside the icon, or more than two states — use SegmentedControl.

disambiguateFrom.distinction: Both are binary and switch-shaped, but semantics differ: Switch is role=switch for a saved on/off SETTING that takes effect immediately (form-adjacent); Toggle is a button+aria-pressed for a toolbar MODE. The sliding-pill shape on Toggle is chosen for icon identity, not to imply a persisted setting. Setting → Switch; mode → Toggle.

Toggle is ONE button (aria-pressed) whose two icons are the two STATES of a single concept; SegmentedControl is N independently-selectable buttons picking one of several parallel OPTIONS, and it carries labels. Two states of one thing → Toggle; one-of-several labeled views → SegmentedControl.
IconButton is a one-shot action with no held state and no track/thumb; Toggle holds a pressed on/off state and renders the sliding-pill track. Action → IconButton; held binary mode → Toggle.

Checkbox is a form selection with deferred submit, indeterminate, and validation; Toggle is an immediate icon-only mode with none of those. Deferred form choice → Checkbox; live toolbar mode → Toggle.

items.name: menu
items.title: Menu
items.description: A floating panel of contextual actions opened from a trigger. Built on Radix UI with leading/trailing icon slots, an optional description line, section headings, checkbox and radio items, submenus, keyboard-shortcut hints, and a destructive variant. The canonical Arbor menu surface.

useWhen: Opening a floating panel of contextual actions, commands, or navigation from a trigger you control via asChild.
Rendering rows with a leading icon, an optional secondary description line, a trailing supporting hint or keyboard shortcut, and a destructive variant.
Toggling settings inline via checkbox or radio items, where the choice is a command not a submitted form value.
Grouping related actions under non-focusable section headings, separated by MenuDivider.
notWhen: Selecting a value for a form field from a list — use Select or SearchInput instead.
Right-click / context menus — the context-menu type is deferred in v1; compose the Radix `@radix-ui/react-context-menu` primitive directly until Menu ships it.
Nesting more than 2 submenu levels — switch to a tree, cascading panels, or a dedicated page.
Showing a single hover hint or arbitrary interactive content — use Tooltip or RichTooltip instead.

disambiguateFrom.distinction: Select picks a value for a form field; Menu fires actions and toggles. Use Select when the result is a submitted value, Menu for an action menu.

ContextMenu opens on right-click at the cursor; Menu v1 opens from a button trigger. The context-menu type is deferred — use the Radix `@radix-ui/react-context-menu` primitive directly for right-click menus.

Popover (deprecated) holds arbitrary interactive content; Menu is a roving-focus list of items. Use Menu for an action list; for forms or free-form anchored layout there is no approved component — escalate to the Design System team.

items.name: avatar
items.title: Avatar
items.description: User avatar with image, fallback, badge, and overflow-group composition. Five sizes and three shapes (circle, squircle, square).

useWhen: Representing a person or account with a photo, initials, or icon fallback (xs/sm/md/lg/xl).
Showing presence or status on an avatar via the AvatarBadge dot in a corner.
Stacking several people in an overlapping row with AvatarGroup and an AvatarGroupCount overflow tally.
Matching a surface's shape with circle, squircle, or square avatars.
notWhen: Labeling a count, status word, or category as text — use Badge (StatusBadge/PlanBadge).
Flagging unread items on an icon or button — use NotificationBadge.
Showing a loading placeholder while the avatar resolves — use SkeletonAvatar.
Rendering a plain UI glyph with no person behind it — use an icon from components/icons.
Showing a brand or service logo — use AppIcon.

disambiguateFrom.distinction: Badge is a small text/status label (StatusBadge, PlanBadge); Avatar represents a person or account image. Pick Badge for words/counts, Avatar for identity.
NotificationBadge is the unread dot/count overlay on an icon or button; AvatarBadge is Avatar's own presence/status dot. Use AvatarBadge inside an Avatar, NotificationBadge elsewhere.
AppIcon renders a brand/service logo at a fixed size; Avatar renders a person or account portrait with initials/icon fallback. Use AppIcon for a product mark, Avatar for identity imagery.
SkeletonAvatar is the shimmer placeholder shown before the image loads; Avatar is the resolved element. Render SkeletonAvatar during loading, Avatar once data arrives.
A 'chip' or 'pill' is a compact labeled token — that is Badge or a small Button in Arbor, not Avatar. Use Badge/Button for a token, Avatar for an identity image.
External term for the picture itself. Arbor's Avatar is the component that renders it with AvatarImage plus an initials/icon fallback; use Avatar — there is no separate 'profile picture' component.

items.name: alert
items.title: Alert
items.description: Inline status message with five statuses (info, success, warning, error, neutral), primary or secondary visual variants, and an optional dismiss action.

useWhen: A form submission fails and the error must stay visible above the form until it's fixed.
A persistent system condition needs to stay on the page (plan limit reached, service degradation, beta notice).
A status message is too long or important to trust to a 5-second toast.
A contextual warning belongs alongside a specific section and should be announced to screen readers.
notWhen: Feedback is transient and the action already completed ('Profile saved', 'Link copied') — use Toast.
Someone must explicitly confirm or cancel a destructive action — use AlertDialog.
Guidance is per-field and always applies regardless of input — use Field description (inline helper text).
You'd let someone dismiss an unresolved error — omit onDismiss so the alert persists until fixed.

disambiguateFrom.distinction: Toast auto-dismisses and overlays the viewport; Alert persists in page flow and announces assertively for error/warning. Pick Alert when missing the message would cause a problem, Toast for transient confirmation.
AlertDialog is a modal that blocks until someone confirms or cancels; Alert never blocks and requires no decision. Pick AlertDialog for destructive confirmations, Alert to inform in place.

Field description is static per-field guidance; Alert is a page- or section-level status surface for multi-field or system errors. Pick Field text for single-field validation, Alert for broader status.
What Polaris/Atlassian call a 'banner' is Arbor's Alert — an inline persistent status surface. Use Alert; there is no separate Banner component.

items.name: toast
items.title: Toast
items.description: Notification toast built on Sonner with default and inverse surfaces, optional icon, action button, and stacked chin decoration.

useWhen: Confirm a completed action with ambient, self-dismissing feedback (saved, copied, sent).
Surface a transient success, info, or warning that does not block what someone is doing.
Offer one optional follow-up action like undo or retry alongside brief copy.
Send programmatically via sendToast / sendToastSuccess outside React render.
notWhen: A blocking error or destructive confirmation needs a decision — use Dialog or AlertDialog (assertive, focused).
The message must stay visible and persist on the page — use Alert inline instead.
The only way to reach an action is the toast and it auto-dismisses — put the action elsewhere too.
Validation belongs next to a field — use Field error text, not a toast.

disambiguateFrom.distinction: Alert is a persistent inline notification that stays in the layout; Toast is ambient and auto-dismisses. Pick Alert when the message must remain visible, Toast for transient feedback.
Dialogs interrupt with focus and demand a choice (assertive); Toast announces politely and never blocks. Pick a dialog for errors or confirmations needing action, Toast for low-stakes status.
Tooltip explains an element on hover/focus and is anchored to it; Toast is an unanchored, time-boxed system notification. Pick Tooltip for contextual hints, Toast for action confirmation.
Snackbar is the Material name for this same pattern. In Arbor it is Toast — built on Sonner with default/inverse surfaces. Use Toast.
A banner is a page-level persistent message bar; Toast is transient and floats over content. Use Alert for banner-style notices, Toast for ephemeral feedback.

items.name: native-select
items.title: NativeSelect
items.description: Native HTML select styled with Arbor design tokens. Use when platform select behaviour is preferred over a custom dropdown.

useWhen: The form is simple, mobile-first, or data-dense and benefits from OS-native pickers.
You want maximum platform consistency and native scroll/selection behavior.
The list has 4 to ~10 options that need no custom rendering.
You want field error state to flow automatically via the Field component.
notWhen: You need grouped visual labels, icons, or custom item rendering — use Select (custom).
People must search or filter a long list — use Combobox.
Fewer than 4 options — use RadioGroup or SegmentedControl.
